headline: MEIC, the strategy trading real money, had a good week: +$1,696 after fees. Tonight's research tested 28 strategy ideas. None is ready for you: the one that looked like a winner was a data error, caught by our checks.

decisions.title: Should we test a "volatility check" before our options trades?
detail: **What it is:** before MEIC, MNG or FLY opens a trade, compare how far the market has really moved over the last 5 days with how far the options market expected it to move. Then trade normal size, smaller, or skip the day.
**Why now:** it was the best new options idea tonight (29.5 of 40 points; 28+ means worth testing). It is backed by a 193-day study of SPY options and an April 2026 academic paper.
**The catch:** a quick look at our own 45 days of data shows the opposite of the paper's claim. MEIC earned more after the market moved MORE than expected.
**Recommendation:** approve a paper-only study. I fix which direction to test before looking at more data, so we can't fool ourselves. No real money is involved.

decisions.title: Should we stop running MEP (and keep MPM and OCB)?
detail: **What they are:** three experiments that run in the paper lab but are not in its official line-up:
• **MEP** sells only the downside (put) half of MEIC, in the afternoon.
• **MPM** does the same in the morning.
• **OCB** trades only upward breakouts after the first half-hour.

**The numbers:** MEP has lost **$3,433** over 57 trades. It earns only 54 cents for every dollar it loses, the worst record in the lab. MPM is roughly flat (+$189 over 48 trades). OCB is +$1,305, but over only 7 trades, too few to judge.
**Recommendation:** retire MEP. Keep MPM and OCB on paper until each has about 100 trades.

decisions.title: Please confirm the interest rates the currency strategies use
detail: **Why it matters:** the currency "carry" strategies buy currencies with high interest rates and sell those with low rates, so they need each country's central-bank rate. Those rates are still placeholder numbers from setup, so this month's carry results can't be trusted.
**What to do:** open paper.sahmi.ae/fx, check the policy-rate table against current central-bank rates, correct anything wrong, then reply.

sections.title: Research · new strategy ideas (stocks, bonds, currencies, commodities, crypto)

items: Five research agents, one per asset class, searched academic papers, journals and practitioner research. They found 100 ideas and scored each out of 100.
The best 25, plus 3 re-tests I chose, were backtested on 20–40 years of data.

To be recommended to you, an idea must beat its benchmark with 99% statistical confidence. It must also keep winning in the most recent 30% of the data, which it never saw while being designed. It must clear five further checks used by professional quant firms: luck-adjusted returns, strength of evidence, double trading costs, nearby settings, and not just repackaging a known factor.
Finally, a separate "red team" agent tries to break any winner.

rows: Stocks
16 + 3 re-tests
Bonds
Currencies
Commodities & futures
Crypto

items: **Greenblatt "magic formula" (buy good companies at cheap prices) · NEAR MISS.** We tested it properly for the first time. The data includes companies that later went bust, and uses only the financial figures known at each date. From 2000 to 2024 it made **14.2% a year vs 7.6% for the S&P 500**. It cleared every professional check, including showing real skill rather than a known factor. It failed one test: from 2017 to 2024, when a few giant tech stocks drove the market, it lagged. It goes on the shortlist as a building block. Next I will test it with a trend filter to soften its 57% fall in 2008.

**High-yield bond trend (own junk bonds only when they are rising) · LOOKED LIKE A WINNER, BROKEN BY THE RED TEAM.** It passed every check on the Vanguard high-yield fund's price history. The red team found that this fund's daily prices lag the real market by about a day. That lag makes a trend rule look brilliant on paper, but you could never trade it. On the real, tradeable ETF (HYG) the edge mostly disappears: it only softens crashes a little. Rejected. Lesson recorded: test illiquid assets on tradeable ETFs only.

**Stock momentum (buy the past year's winners) · FAIL.** This is the strategy that once looked great and was later stopped. On honest data it made 9.1% a year vs 7.6% for the S&P. That gain is entirely the well-known "momentum factor", with no extra skill. The old success came from testing only on companies that survived.

blocks.text: **Other ideas tested (all failed on their own):** several are useful as crash protection or as small, independent pieces of a bigger portfolio.

items: **Crypto:** a Bitcoin trend filter with risk-based sizing cut the worst loss from −83% to −46%, but made less money than simply holding Bitcoin.
**Commodities:** owning them only when their trend is up AND inflation-protected bonds beat ordinary bonds cut the worst loss from −76% to −31%.
**Bonds:** holding Treasuries only over the last 3 days of each month earned the same as always holding them, at a quarter of the risk.
**Most stock-picking "secrets" are well-known factors in disguise.** On honest data, only quality-plus-value showed real skill.
**Stale prices create fake winners.** Every illiquid-asset idea is now tested on a tradeable ETF.
**Crash protection is reliable in every asset class; beating buy-and-hold is not.** These rules are best used as a safety layer.

**Small edges work as a team.** Ten new building blocks went on the shortlist. Combined, nine of them made a steady low-risk portfolio: 3.8% a year with only 2.5% volatility, a Sharpe ratio of 1.51 (excellent risk-adjusted). The next step is to combine them deliberately.
